title: Localization in tight-binding models with power-law distributed couplings
authors: Maximilian Weigmann, Luca Schaefer, Barbara Drossel
abstract: We study the localization properties of 1D and 2D tight-binding models with power-law distributed couplings by comparing the spectrum and the localization properties of the eigenmodes of the Laplacian and the adjacency matrix, using numerical diagonalization of these matrices for different system sizes and connectivities. These two matrices are relevant for different types of dynamical processes. While all eigenmodes of the adjacency matrix are localized for sufficiently large system sizes, the Laplacian matrix always leads to a small proportion of system-spanning modes due to a conservation law, and therefore to power-law tails in the probability distribution of the participation ratio and its relation to the eigenvalues. In one dimension, the exponent of these power laws change continuously with the exponent that characterizes the distribution of couplings. In two dimensions, the modes with the largest relaxation times change from system-spanning to localized when the exponent of the distribution of couplings becomes larger than 0.75. We provide phenomenological explanations for all these findings.
summary: This work investigates how disorder, characterized by power-law couplings, affects electron localization in 1D and 2D tight-binding models. By comparing the Laplacian and adjacency matrices, the authors show that while the adjacency matrix always yields localized modes, the Laplacian reveals system-spanning modes due to conservation laws. The critical finding is a dimension-dependent transition point in 2D that dictates when transport shifts from extended to localized behavior.
main_problem: The study investigates the localization properties of one-dimensional and two-dimensional tight-binding models subjected to power-law distributed couplings.
main_result: The Laplacian matrix always yields system-spanning modes due to conservation laws, while the localization behavior in 2D depends critically on the coupling exponent $s$, transitioning from system-spanning to localized modes when $s > 0.75$.
method: The analysis employs numerical diagonalization of the adjacency and Laplacian matrices, calculating diagnostics like the Participation Ratio ($P_i$) and analyzing the resulting probability distribution functions (PDFs) and density of states (DOS).
model_or_system: The models are 1D and 2D tight-binding systems featuring power-law distributed couplings $f(t) \sim t^{-s}$. Two primary Hamiltonians are analyzed: the Random-Coupling Model (RCM) using the weighted adjacency matrix, and the Diffusion Model (DM) using the discretized Laplacian matrix.
key_observables: Participation Ratio ($P_i$), Probability Distribution of $P$ ($	ext{PDF}(P)$), Density of States ($	ext{DOS}(E)$), and the relation between $P$ and $E$.
important_parameters: The power-law exponent $s$ (controlling disorder strength), system dimension (1D vs. 2D), and system size $N$.
main_assumptions: The analysis distinguishes between RCM (bond disorder) and DM (site/bond disorder correlated via $\sum_m t_{nm} = 0$), and it notes that finite-size effects are a consideration.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the $	ext{PDF}(P)$, $	ext{DOS}(E)$, and $P$ vs $E$ relationships for 1D and 2D systems, showing how these distributions change as the disorder exponent $s$ is varied.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the localization diagnostics (Participation Ratio, DOS) between the Laplacian (DM) and the Adjacency matrix (RCM) in 1D and 2D. It derives specific power-law behaviors for the PDF of $P$ in 1D and identifies critical thresholds for mode localization in 2D.
why_interesting: The study provides quantitative, dimension-dependent criteria ($s > 0.75$ in 2D) for the transition between delocalized and localized transport regimes in disordered lattices, which has implications for understanding energy/heat transport in disordered materials.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Probability distribution of the participation ratio (top), density of states (middle), and relation between participation ratio and eigenvalue (bottom) for the 1D diffusion model. The left graphs show the data for different power law exponents s, the right graphs show the data for different system sizes, for a large (s = 0.8) and a small value (s = 0.0) of s. The tilted dashed lines indicate power laws obtained from theoretical considerations; the horizontal dashed lines indicate the participation ratio of sine functions, which prevail for large wavelengths.

Figure 2: Probability distribution of the participation ratio (top), density of states (middle), and relation between participation ratios and eigenvalues (bottom) for the 1D random-coupling model. The graphs on the left show the data for different power law exponents s, the graphs on the right show the data for different system sizes, for a large (s = 0.8) and a small value (s = 0.0) of s. The dashed line represents the Dyson singularity ∼(E ln3 E)−1.

Figure 3: Density of states of the 2D diffusion model for s = 0 and N = 2500. The vertical dashed lines indicate the lowest eigenvalues of the system without disorder, where the eigenmodes are products of sine functions.

Figure 4: Probability distribution of the participation ratio (top), density of states (middle), and relation between participation ratio and eigenvalue (bottom) for the 2D diffusion model. The left graphs show the data for different power law exponents s, the right graphs show the data for different system sizes, for a large and a small values of s. The dashed lines in the top row show the theoretically predicted exponent −1.5.

Figure 5: Each eigenmode of the 2D diffusion model is represented by a dot in the P-E plane, with the color indicating the density of dots. The system size is N = 15625, the power-law exponent is s = 0.0 on the left and s = 0.85 on the right.
